podcast.title: Internet Unprofitability of In Rainbows (2007)
podcast.body: Despite the success of the "In Rainbows" pay-what-you-want model, it was later revealed that 60% of the traffic to inrainbows.com resulted in no profit for the band beyond the credit card processing fees, as users either paid only the minimum or downloaded the album from torrent sites after it was in the wild. "That means 60% of the traffic to in rainbows.com was unprofitable for everybody but the credit card companies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Music Industry Chaos (2007)
podcast.body: In 2007, the music industry was in turmoil due to the internet's disruptive impact, rampant music piracy, and plummeting CD sales, leading to widespread uncertainty about how musicians could generate income from recorded music. This unstable environment provided the context for Radiohead's bold experiments in distribution. "The whole industry was in chaos thanks to the disruption by the internet. Music piracy was rampant, CD sales were falling, no one had any idea of how anyone was going to make money from recorded music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 8: (30-21)

podcast.title: Pioneering "Tip Jar" Pricing (2007)
podcast.body: With their 2007 album *In Rainbows*, Radiohead pioneered an innovative "tip jar" pricing model for digital versions, allowing fans to pay "anything you want for it." This strategy, combined with a deluxe physical set, reportedly resulted in the band earning more money than from any previous release, including *OK Computer*, despite many choosing to pay nothing. "In Rainbows pioneered the tip jar approach. Here's the record. You can get various forms of it online, and you can pay anything you want for it. Even though thousands chose to pay nothing for the record, it was reported that Radiohead ended up making more money from In Rainbows than they did from any other release in their career."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Radical Independent Experiment (2007)
podcast.body: After their impasse with EMI, Radiohead decided to go "totally, utterly, 100% independent," embarking on a daring experiment to release music digitally, without a traditional label. This allowed them to retain full ownership of their work (publishing, masters, copyright), a level of control typically unattainable under label deals, and enabled them to explore innovative distribution models like the "pay-what-you-want" approach for "In Rainbows." "Radiohead went totally, utterly, 100% independent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Self-Leak Strategy for In Rainbows (2007)
podcast.body: To counter unauthorized leaks and maintain artistic integrity, Radiohead secretly decided to "leak their own album" (In Rainbows) by releasing it directly to fans online through a pay-what-you-want model. This innovative approach allowed them to control the terms of release and bypass traditional distribution challenges. "As Tom York said to Wired Magazine, we are going to leak our own album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Independent Operations (Since 2008)
podcast.body: Radiohead has chosen to operate as an independent entity since 2008, managing all their projects without the involvement of major record labels. They conduct all their business "on their own and on their own terms," indicating a deliberate move away from the traditional music industry system. "Radiohead has no use for the major label system anymore, and does everything on their own and on their own terms."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-In Rainbows Public Silence (2008-2010)
podcast.body: After the "In Rainbows" experiment, Radiohead largely withdrew from the public eye for a couple of years, preferring to communicate through social media and their websites, with no live gigs for over a year, and band members exploring individual projects. During this time, EMI, asserting its rights, released a box set of Radiohead's previous six albums and a greatest hits CD. "There were no Radiohead gigs for over a year. And they also decided to explore various things as individuals."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The King of Limbs Recording Location Rumors (Early 2010)
podcast.body: Most of "The King of Limbs" was recorded in Los Angeles over nearly two years, with rumors suggesting the band set up a studio at actress Drew Barrymore's home in the Hollywood Hills in early 2010. While unconfirmed, the album's liner notes included an "ecliptic thank you," and social media showed pictures and celebrity party rumors from the house. "Most of the recording seems to have been done in Los Angeles, with rumors saying that they'd set up at the home of actress Drew Barrymore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The King of Limbs - Stanley Donwood's Newspaper Edition (March 28, 2011)
podcast.body: As part of the release for "The King of Limbs," longtime collaborator Stanley Donwood created the "Newspaper edition." This included a newspaper-like insert designed to fade when exposed to sunlight, serving as a metaphor for the natural decay of living things. This was published under the name "Universal Sigh" and was distributed as a free paper at indie record stores worldwide on March 28, 2011, filled with poetry, lyrics, artwork, and short stories. "There was something called the Newspaper edition created by longtime artwork collaborator Stanley Donwood. It came with a newspaper like Insert, which was designed to fade when exposed to sunlight, thereby creating a metaphor for the natural decay of living things or something of that sort."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Downsview Park Stage Collapse (June 16, 2012)
podcast.body: On Saturday, June 16, 2012, a stage under construction for a Radiohead concert at Downsview Park in Toronto collapsed around 4:00 PM, an hour before the gates were scheduled to open and just before the band's soundcheck. The stage roof fell, crushing Phil Selba's drum tech, Scott Johnson, with a 5,000-pound video monitor, killing him. Three other people were injured, one seriously, and much of the band's lighting and stage gear was destroyed. "On Saturday, June 16, 2012, a stage was almost finished being built at Downsview Park in Toronto ahead of that night's gig, headlined by Radiohead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Downsview Park Stage Collapse (June 16, 2012)
podcast.body: A temporary stage, built by Toronto firm Optex for a Radiohead concert at Downsview Park in Toronto, collapsed on Saturday, June 16, 2012, approximately an hour before gates were scheduled to open and minutes before the band's soundcheck. The structure, approved by certified engineers and with permits in place, was designed to hold 7,700 kilograms of equipment. Despite prior inspections, the roof suddenly crashed down, bringing the entire top of the structure with it. Radiohead's drum tech, Scott Johnson, who had been with the band for about two years, was tragically crushed to death by a 2,300-kilogram video monitor. Three other crew members were injured, one seriously. The concert was canceled, and the aftermath involved a protracted "comedy of errors" with inquests, lawsuits, court cases, delays, and dismissals that were not fully resolved until late 2020. The tragedy led to the implementation of new safety standards for temporary concert stages, though many felt justice was not adequately served. "Scott Johnson, Phil Selway's drum tech, who had been with the band for about two years, was crushed by a video monitor that weighed almost 2,300 kilograms."

podcast.title: Toronto Stage Collapse Tragedy (June 16, 2012)
podcast.body: A catastrophic stage collapse occurred at Downsview Park in Toronto on June 16, 2012, shortly before a Radiohead concert. A temporary stage structure, supporting 7,000 kilos of gear, gave way, killing 33-year-old drum tech Scott Johnson, who was struck by a 2,270-kilo video monitor, and injuring three other crew members. The band's light show and most of their musical gear were destroyed. If the crew had been on schedule, Radiohead would have been sound-checking at the time of the collapse. "a part of the stage constructed for that night's gig, a structured laden with 7,000 kilos of gear suddenly gave way, plummeting to the ground, and killing 33-year-old drum tech Scott Johnson"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Spectre" Theme Release as Free Download (2015)
podcast.body: After their song "Spectre" was rejected as the theme for the James Bond film, Radiohead released it as a free download through SoundCloud when the movie opened. It was also made available on B-sides and bonus tracks, allowing fans to access their unreleased Bond theme. "They ended up releasing that as a free download through SoundCloud when the movie opened."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Bookies Bet on Radiohead for "Spectre" (2015)
podcast.body: There were strong rumors that Radiohead had secured the job for the "Spectre" theme, leading British bookmakers to halt bets. Many people were placing money on 10-to-1 odds for Radiohead, reflecting significant public and industry belief in their selection before Sam Smith was officially announced. "British bookies had to stop making bets because so many people were putting down money on a 10-to-1 odds against Radiohead getting the gig."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Istanbul Listening Session Attack (June 17, 2016)
podcast.body: On June 17, 2016, the day "A Moon-Shaped Pool" was physically released, an organized listening session at an indie record store in Istanbul, Turkey, was attacked by a gang. The attackers reportedly believed the shop should not have been playing music or serving beer during Ramadan. Fortunately, no one was injured during the incident. "A series of listening sessions had been organized at indie record stores around the world, and a shop in Istanbul, Turkey, was attacked by a gang who somehow believed that the shop shouldn't be playing music or serving beer during Ramadan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Thom Yorke's Personal Tragedy (2016)
podcast.body: Thom Yorke and his partner, Rachel, separated after 16 years. A few months after the release of "A Moon-Shaped Pool" in December 2016, Rachel tragically died of cancer. "Another sad thing, Tom York and his partner Rachel separated after 16 years, and then she died of cancer that December, a few months after the album came out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Return to Toronto and Memorial (July 19, 2018)
podcast.body: Radiohead did not perform in Toronto again until July 19, 2018, six years after the fatal stage collapse. During this concert, with the legal case still stalled, Thom Yorke publicly addressed the situation from the stage, and the band observed a moment of silence for Scott Johnson before continuing their performance. "Radiohead didn't play Toronto again until July 19, 2018."

podcast.title: "Burn the Witch" Video Copyright Accusation
podcast.body: Radiohead faced accusations of copyright infringement for the distinctive style in which the music video for their song "Burn the Witch" was shot. "And then Radiohead was accused of breach of copyright for the style in which the Burn the Witch video was shot."

podcast.body: "Fitter Happier" was initially considered as the opening track for the *OK Computer* album. However, it was ultimately decided that the song was "too much of a downer" to begin the album, so it was placed as track seven instead. "It almost ended up as the opening track for okay computer But was considered too much of a downer so it ended up as track seven"

podcast.title: "Great Creative Explosion" Era (Kid A, Amnesiac, Hail to the Thief)
podcast.body: The period spanning `Kid A`, `Amnesiac`, and `Hail to the Thief` is described as Thom Yorke's most significant creative explosion, characterized by marathon recording sessions over months that generated thousands of hours of material. This intense process, while creatively fruitful, left the band emotionally drained. "la mayor explosión creativa que tuvo Tom Jorken toda su vida fue la que grabó en la gran triilogía del quidad de la amnesia y de la emite y ron ahí se grabaron durante meses sesiones maratonianas en las que se juntaron miles de horas de grabaciones."

podcast.body: A theory suggests that "OK Computer" (designated as 01) and "In Rainbows" (designated as 10) can be combined into one "mega album" by creating a playlist that alternates tracks from each album, with a ten-second cross-fade between songs. "If we designate Ok Computer as zero one, and in Rainbows as one zero, the two albums can be combined to create one mega album."

podcast.title: "On a Friday" Name Origin
podcast.body: The band originally adopted the name "On a Friday" because Friday was the sole day of the week when all the members could gather for rehearsals. "As it turns out, the only day the guys could rehearse was Friday. So the band became known as on a Friday."

podcast.title: "The Untitled Radiohead Project" Play
podcast.body: Dean Testerman, a Los Angeles-based director, playwright, and freelance journalist, created a play titled "The Untitled Radiohead Project" where all dialogue was exclusively taken from Radiohead song lyrics. The narrative centered on a young man named Tom who, after a car crash, examines his life subconsciously while in a coma. Although planned for small 70-seat theaters in Los Angeles with potential for venues in Vancouver and Toronto, the production was halted by Radiohead's copyright lawyers because Testerman had not obtained permission to use their lyrics. "All the dialogue in the Untitled Radiohead Project is taken from Radiohead songs."

podcast.title: "Theory of Ten" for In Rainbows
podcast.body: The release of "In Rainbows" was surrounded by a playful "Theory of Ten," noting its release ten years after "OK Computer," on the 10th day of the 10th month of 2007, announced ten days after its initial mention, and following ten cryptic messages on the band's website using the Roman numeral 'X'. Even the album's working title, "Zero's and One's," mirrored the number ten. "In Rainbows came out ten years after Ok Computer. It was released on the 10th day of the 10th month of 2007. It was released ten days after was announced, and following ten cryptic messages posted on the band's website."

podcast.title: "Tip Jar" Distribution Model
podcast.body: In October 2007, Radiohead famously launched their "In Rainbows" album with a "pay-what-you-want" model. This allowed fans to download the record and decide how much, if anything, they wanted to pay, representing a significant challenge to conventional music pricing and distribution. "Pay whatever you want for it. If you choose to pay nothing, well, you know what, that's your choice."

podcast.body: Radiohead is mentioned as one of the "big bands" that experienced a resurgence in activity around 2000-2001, helping rock music regain its public dominance.

podcast.title: 21st Century Legacy Artist
podcast.body: Radiohead is recognized as a "legacy artist" who continues to leverage their music to advocate for change in the 21st century, in contrast to many newer artists who tend to shy away from overt political statements. "it's legacy artists, radio heads, Springsteen, U2, that continue to push for change through music while newer artists generally stay away from this area."

podcast.title: A Moon-Shaped Pool's Low-Key Promotion
podcast.body: The release of "A Moon-Shaped Pool" was marked by a minimalist promotional approach: there were no interviews, and none of the songs had been road-tested in advance. podcast.title: Advance and Copyright Deadlock with EMI
podcast.body: Radiohead, after having sold 25 million records and delivered tens of millions in revenue to EMI since 1992, requested an advance of £10 million for a new contract, but EMI would not offer more than £3 million. Crucially, EMI also refused to grant Radiohead any control over their back catalog's copyright, insisting on retaining rights for the standard 50 years, leading to an insurmountable deadlock. "Radiohead also wanted some measure of control over their back catalog and how that music would be exploited going forward. But EMI would not budge."

podcast.title: Aftermath of Toronto Stage Collapse
podcast.body: The Toronto show was canceled, and Scott Johnson's death devastated everyone involved. Scott Johnson's father, Ken Johnson, an expert in scaffolding health and safety, had "no doubt why the accident happened." xref.title: Prolific Songwriter
xref.body: Albert Hammond Sr. is a successful songwriter who wrote numerous songs for a wide array of prominent artists. His credits include songs for Celine Dion, Aretha Franklin, Whitney Houston, Willie Nelson, Chicago, and The Carpenters. He also received a writing credit on Radiohead's song "Creep" due to its melodic resemblance to "The Air That I Breathe," a song he wrote for The Hollies in the 1970s, as determined by a court case. "He wrote this song. Dad also wrote songs for Celine Dion, where we at the Franklin Whitney Houston, Willie Nelson, Chicago, the Carpenter, and a ton of others."

xref.title: Restlessness and Work Ethic
xref.body: Yorke is described as a workaholic who constantly needs to make music. When Radiohead took time between albums after their record deal ended, he used this period to work on his solo material. "He's one of those guys who always has to keep making music."

xref.title: Stage Fright and Writer's Block
xref.body: As a member of Radiohead, Yorke faced significant obligations and pressures which occasionally led to paralyzing cases of stage fright and writer's block. xref.title: Studio Two Notable Clients
xref.body: Beyond The Beatles, Studio Two has hosted a legendary array of artists, including Pink Floyd, Oasis, Muse, Elbow, Iron Maiden, The Killers, The Hollies, Radiohead, and U2. "Pink Floyd, Oasis, Muse, Elbow, Iron Maiden, The Killers, The Hollies, Radiohead, U2."

xref.title: Support for Radiohead
xref.body: Michael Stipe of R.E.M. took Radiohead "under REM's wing" and offered them support slots on their tour, which was a "huge, huge help" for Radiohead's exposure and provided them with advice. The bands "got along famously" and exchanged pranks on tour, such as Michael Stipe sending a radio-controlled car onto the stage during Radiohead's set. "It never really caught on until Michael Steip took Radiohead under REM's wing and offered them support slots on their monster tour."
